explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The LORD doesn't tell David to wait. He answers, “Go up.” That's two words, and I've watched whole batches rise slower than that.
That's right. David asks if he should go up to one of the towns of Judah, and the LORD answers, “Go up.” It's a short, clear yes. No waiting, no guessing, and David gets to ask his next question.
Yes, baker! David asks, “Where should I go?” and the LORD replies, “To Hebron.” David asks a clear question and gets a clear answer. I wish my recipe cards were that direct.
Bethlehem is a good guess, since it's David's hometown. But the text never sends him there. The LORD replies, “To Hebron.” That's the town David heads for.

Keilah is a real town, but it's not the one the LORD names here. David asks where he should go, and the LORD replies, “To Hebron.” One question, one town, no detours. Even my kitchen GPS wishes it were that simple.

explanations.answer: His two wives Ahinoam and Abigail
explanations.explanation: That's it. The text says David went to Hebron “with his two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel.” Ahinoam and Abigail go up with him. David asks the LORD where to go, and then he doesn't go alone.

explanations.answer: His father Jesse and his brothers
explanations.explanation: Jesse was David's father and his brothers were part of the family, but this passage doesn't say they go to Hebron. It names two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel. Then it adds the men who were with David and their households. Look at that list, friend, and keep the names straight.

explanations.answer: The prophet Samuel and the priests
explanations.explanation: Samuel was the prophet who anointed David years ago (1 Samuel 16:13), but he isn't in this move. The text says David went with his two wives, Ahinoam and Abigail. His men and their households come next. Priests aren't on the list, and I checked it twice, like a baker with a timer.

explanations.answer: Anoint him king over the house of Judah
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! The text says, “there they anointed David king over the house of Judah.” They come to Hebron and make it official. David is king, and he's been doing his best baking in the Lord's will the whole time.

explanations.answer: Ask him to lead them against the Philistines
explanations.explanation: Nope, friend. The Philistines aren't mentioned in this passage at all. What the men of Judah do in Hebron is anoint David king over the house of Judah. That's the big moment here.

explanations.answer: Hand him the crown from Saul's head
explanations.explanation: Good try, but there's no crown handoff in these verses. The men of Judah anoint David king over the house of Judah, right there in Hebron. The text only tells us about anointing, not a crown. I'd have tried to hand over a cookie.
That's right! The men of Judah tell David, “It was the men of Jabesh-gilead who buried Saul.” That's a heavy piece of news. David hears it and acts on it right away, as the next verses show.

Ziklag is not the town in this verse. The men of Judah tell David it was the men of Jabesh-gilead who buried Saul. It's a tricky name, and I once mixed up two spice jars myself. The name to hold on to is Jabesh-gilead.

Ramah isn't named here. The men of Judah tell David, “It was the men of Jabesh-gilead who buried Saul.” That's the news David gets, and he sends messengers because of it. Say it with me: Jabesh-gilead.

explanations.answer: The LORD bless you for your kindness to Saul
explanations.explanation: That's the one. David tells them, “The LORD bless you, because you showed this kindness to Saul your lord when you buried him.” He sends a blessing to the men who buried Saul. He calls it kindness, and I think that's a nice way to say thanks.

explanations.answer: The LORD guard you as you mourn for Saul
explanations.explanation: That's a thoughtful line, but it isn't what David says. His message is, “The LORD bless you, because you showed this kindness to Saul your lord when you buried him.” He names their kindness, the burial itself. Nothing in the verse mentions guarding them.

explanations.answer: The LORD reward you for joining my army
explanations.explanation: Close to the sound of it, but no. The men of Jabesh-gilead aren't called soldiers in this message. David says, “The LORD bless you, because you showed this kindness to Saul your lord when you buried him.” The kindness is the burial.

That's right. David says, “I will also show you the same favor because you have done this.” He asks the LORD to show them loving devotion and faithfulness, and he adds a promise of his own. A kind word and a promise to match, and I'd bake a whole batch for that.

It's actually true, friend. In verse 6, David says, “I will also show you the same favor because you have done this.” So David adds his own promise to his blessing. Read that line again, and it's right there.

Yes, baker! David says, “be strong and courageous, for though Saul your lord is dead, the house of Judah has anointed me as their king.” Saul is dead, and David tells the men of Jabesh-gilead about it. Strong and courageous, that's his message.
Quiet and careful sounds sensible, but that's not David's message. He says, “be strong and courageous.” That's a bolder pair of words. I'm usually quiet and careful only when I'm near a hot oven.

That's a calm answer, but David's words are different. He tells the men of Jabesh-gilead, “be strong and courageous.” Then he tells them the house of Judah has anointed him as their king. Strong and courageous is what the text says.
That's right! Abner son of Ner, the commander of Saul's army, takes Saul's son Ish-bosheth and moves him to Mahanaim. Saul's side has a plan of its own. Abner is the one making the move.

Ziba isn't in these verses. Abner, the commander of Saul's army, takes Saul's son Ish-bosheth and moves him to Mahanaim. It's Saul's own son, and not a servant, who gets moved. Abner is a man with a plan.
Abiathar isn't in this passage. Abner, the commander of Saul's army, takes Saul's son Ish-bosheth and moves him to Mahanaim. That's the person Abner moves. Keep your eye on the king's son, friend.
That's it! Abner makes Ish-bosheth king over Gilead, Asher, Jezreel, Ephraim and Benjamin, “over all Israel.” That's quite a list of places. I can barely get my sprinkle jars in order.

Judah is the wrong place to look here, friend. The text says Ish-bosheth is made king “over all Israel.” In the same passage, the house of Judah anointed David and followed him. Two different groups are going two different ways.

Moab is a good name, but it's not in this verse. Abner makes Ish-bosheth king over Gilead, Asher, Jezreel, Ephraim and Benjamin, “over all Israel.” Israel is the word that finishes the sentence. Moab is a neighboring land, and it's not in this passage.
Not quite, friend. The text says, “The house of Judah, however, followed David.” Ish-bosheth is king over all Israel, but Judah stays with David. That little word “however” is doing a lot of work.

That's right! Verse 10 says, “The house of Judah, however, followed David.” Ish-bosheth is king over Israel, but Judah follows David. Two kings, two groups, and I'd say that's a lot for one kitchen counter.

Yes, baker! The text says David was king in Hebron over the house of Judah “seven years and six months.” Ish-bosheth reigns two years, so David's time in Hebron is longer. That's a good bit of counting.

Three and a half is a decent guess, but it's short. The text says David was king in Hebron over the house of Judah for seven years and six months. Ish-bosheth's reign is two years. The six months part is right, though, and I'll give you that.

You've got the six months, but the years are off. The text says David was king in Hebron over the house of Judah for seven years and six months. Ish-bosheth reigns two years, so David's time in Hebron is a good deal longer. That's a long stretch, and I wouldn't want to count it on one batch of cookies.
